SPY: An ETF tracking the S&P 500, a broad benchmark of the 500 largest U.S. public companies. Widely used as a proxy for the overall U.S. stock market and as the default benchmark most portfolios are measured against.
DIA: An ETF tracking the Dow Jones Industrial Average, a price-weighted index of 30 large U.S. blue-chip companies. One of the oldest and most-quoted U.S. market indices, though its price-weighting means a higher-priced stock moves it more than a larger but cheaper-priced company would.
QQQ: An ETF tracking the Nasdaq-100, a benchmark of the 100 largest non-financial companies listed on the Nasdaq, heavily weighted toward technology. Closely watched as a gauge of growth-stock and tech-sector sentiment specifically, rather than the broader market.
RSP: An equal-weight ETF tracking the S&P 500, giving each of the 500 companies the same weighting rather than weighting by market cap. Tends to reflect how the "average" stock is doing, since it isn't dominated by the handful of largest companies the way the standard cap-weighted S&P 500 is.
IWM: An ETF tracking the Russell 2000, a benchmark of U.S. small-cap companies. Often watched as a barometer of domestic economic health and risk appetite, since smaller companies are typically more sensitive to the U.S. economy and credit conditions than large multinationals.
MAGS: An ETF holding the "Magnificent Seven" mega-cap technology stocks. A concentrated way to track the small group of companies that have accounted for an outsized share of recent U.S. market gains.
BTC-USD: Bitcoin, the largest cryptocurrency by market capitalization, priced in U.S. dollars. Trades continuously around the clock, including weekends and holidays, unlike traditional stock markets.
ETH-USD: Ethereum, the second-largest cryptocurrency by market capitalization, priced in U.S. dollars. Also the leading blockchain platform for smart contracts and decentralized applications, not just a currency.
GC=F: Gold futures, a contract for the future delivery of gold, widely used as a safe-haven asset and inflation hedge. Demand for gold tends to rise during periods of market stress, high inflation, or a weakening dollar.
SI=F: Silver futures, a contract for the future delivery of silver, used both as a precious metal and an industrial input. Tends to be more volatile than gold, since industrial demand (electronics, solar panels) plays a bigger role in its price alongside its safe-haven use.
CL=F: Crude oil futures (WTI), a contract for the future delivery of West Texas Intermediate crude, a key global energy benchmark. Its price ripples through gasoline costs, inflation expectations, and the margins of transport and airline companies.
HG=F: Copper futures, a contract for the future delivery of copper, often watched as a gauge of global industrial demand. Sometimes nicknamed "Dr. Copper" for its reputation of turning before the broader economy does, since it's used so widely across construction and manufacturing.
ES=F: E-mini S&P 500 futures, a contract tracking the S&P 500 index used to trade or hedge broad market exposure outside regular trading hours. Often used by traders to gauge how the market is likely to open before the regular session begins.
YM=F: E-mini Dow futures, a contract tracking the Dow Jones Industrial Average outside regular trading hours. Reflects sentiment in the same 30 blue-chip companies the Dow itself tracks, ahead of the regular session.
NQ=F: E-mini Nasdaq-100 futures, a contract tracking the Nasdaq-100 index outside regular trading hours. Particularly sensitive to overnight news affecting large technology companies, ahead of the regular session.
XLK: Technology Select Sector SPDR Fund, an ETF tracking S&P 500 technology companies. Covers software, hardware, and semiconductor companies -- one of the largest and most closely watched sector funds given technology's weight in the broader market.
XLC: Communication Services Select Sector SPDR Fund, an ETF tracking S&P 500 communication services companies. Covers major media, telecom, and internet/social-media companies.
XLY: Consumer Discretionary Select Sector SPDR Fund, an ETF tracking S&P 500 consumer discretionary companies. Covers retailers, automakers, and other companies whose sales depend on optional (non-essential) consumer spending.
XLF: Financial Select Sector SPDR Fund, an ETF tracking S&P 500 financial companies. Covers banks, insurers, and other financial institutions -- typically sensitive to interest-rate changes.
XLI: Industrial Select Sector SPDR Fund, an ETF tracking S&P 500 industrial companies. Covers aerospace, defense, machinery, and transportation companies, often tied to the broader economic growth cycle.
XLE: Energy Select Sector SPDR Fund, an ETF tracking S&P 500 energy companies. Covers oil, gas, and energy-services companies -- closely tied to crude oil prices.
XLV: Health Care Select Sector SPDR Fund, an ETF tracking S&P 500 health care companies. Covers pharmaceutical, biotech, and health-services companies, often viewed as a more defensive sector since demand for health care tends to hold up regardless of the economic cycle.
XLP: Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR Fund, an ETF tracking S&P 500 consumer staples companies. Covers food, beverage, and household-goods companies whose products see fairly steady demand regardless of the economic cycle.
XLU: Utilities Select Sector SPDR Fund, an ETF tracking S&P 500 utility companies. Covers electric, gas, and water utilities -- typically viewed as a defensive, income-oriented sector.
XLB: Materials Select Sector SPDR Fund, an ETF tracking S&P 500 materials companies. Covers chemicals, metals, and mining companies tied to industrial and construction demand.
XLRE: Real Estate Select Sector SPDR Fund, an ETF tracking S&P 500 real estate companies. Covers real estate investment trusts (REITs) across property types -- typically sensitive to interest-rate changes.
^VIX: The CBOE Volatility Index, a measure of expected S&P 500 volatility over the next 30 days, often called the market's "fear gauge." Shown directly here: a rising VIX (more fear) reads bearish in red, a falling VIX (a calmer market) reads bullish in green.
FEAR_GREED: A composite gauge of overall market sentiment, ranging from Extreme Fear to Extreme Greed based on several market indicators. Shown as a contrarian signal here: Fear reads bullish in green (a potential buying opportunity), Greed reads bearish in red (a caution sign).
PUT_CALL: The ratio of put options traded to call options traded, used as a gauge of investor sentiment -- a high ratio suggests more hedging or bearishness. Shown as a contrarian signal here: a high ratio (more hedging/fear) reads bullish in green, a low ratio (more greed) reads bearish in red.
